opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few layers to the problem.

The first is descriptive. Most of AI alignment, explicitly or implicitly, adopts what my co-authors and I have called the "preferentist" picture: human values can be adequately represented as preferences, rational action means maximizing the satisfaction of those preferences, and so aligning AI means getting it to learn and optimize our preferences. But preferences are a pretty thin representation of what people actually care about. They don't capture the reasons behind our choices, the ways our values are structured and sometimes incommensurable, or how we form and revise what we want over time. When you compress all of that into a scalar reward or a set of pairwise comparisons, as in RLHF, you lose a lot of the semantic content that tells you *why* something is good or bad. That's exactly the information you need to generalize appropriately to new situations.

The second layer is normative. Even if you could perfectly elicit someone's preferences, it's not obvious that expected utility maximization is the right standard of rationality, either for humans or for AI systems. The coherence arguments for EU theory rely on assumptions, like completeness, that real agents often reasonably violate. If I have values that are genuinely incomparable in some cases, it's not irrational for me to lack a preference between them. And if we build AI systems that are forced to be complete EU maximizers, we may get exactly the kind of single-minded, unboundedly optimizing agents that make alignment hard in the first place.

The third layer, which I think matters most, is about multiple people. Alignment isn't just about one user and one assistant; it's about AI systems operating in a society of people who disagree. The preferentist answer is usually some form of preference aggregation: add up everyone's utilities and maximize. But aggregation runs into well-known impossibility results, and more fundamentally, it treats people's values as inputs to an optimization rather than as claims that need to be reconciled through fair processes.

So the alternative we've been pushing is that, instead of aligning AI to preferences, we should align it to normative standards appropriate to its social role. A general-purpose assistant, for example, should be aligned to the norms we'd expect of a good assistant: honesty, respecting the user's autonomy, not causing harm to third parties. Those norms should themselves be negotiated and agreed upon by the stakeholders affected. That's closer to how we handle this among humans. We don't ask doctors or lawyers to maximize some aggregate utility function. We hold them to role-specific norms and codes of conduct, and within those bounds, they serve the particular people they work with. That framing lets you be pluralistic about people's diverse values while still having a shared foundation of norms that makes cooperation possible. It's also more tractable than trying to solve the full problem of human values all at once.

r001.rationale: The response says preference data compressed into scalar rewards can lose meaning and impair generalization, but it does not clearly state that overoptimizing a learned utility function can fail to achieve what humans actually want because the function is an imperfect proxy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I'd frame it is that there's a kind of default picture in a lot of alignment work, which is that what we're trying to do is build systems that satisfy human preferences, and that the right formal language for that is expected utility theory. The system has some utility function, ideally one that represents what we want, and it acts to maximize expected utility under that function. And I think that picture is actually doing a lot of load-bearing work, often without people noticing it's a substantive philosophical commitment rather than just a neutral technical convenience.

There are a few different limitations I'd point to, and they sort of stack on top of each other.

The first is just descriptive. Humans don't actually have stable, coherent preferences over outcomes that we then act on. Our preferences are context-dependent, they're constructed in the moment, they change as we deliberate, they're often incomplete. So if your alignment target is "the user's preferences," you've already got a problem, because there isn't a single well-defined object there to point at. A lot of the work in inverse reinforcement learning and preference learning handles this by assuming the thing exists and then adding noise models on top, but that's kind of papering over the issue rather than engaging with it.

The second limitation is normative, and I think this is the more important one. Even if we could extract someone's preferences perfectly, it's not obvious that satisfying preferences is what we should want AI systems to do. Preferences can be ill-informed, they can be adaptive to bad circumstances, they can conflict with other people's. And more fundamentally, a lot of what matters in human social life isn't well described as preference satisfaction at all. Think about norms, commitments, rights, roles, obligations. When I promise to do something, the reason I do it isn't that I have a preference for keeping promises that happens to outweigh my other preferences in the moment. It's that I've taken on an obligation, and that obligation structures what counts as a reason for me. The expected utility framework can sort of simulate this by stuffing everything into the utility function, but at that point the framework isn't explaining anything, it's just a bookkeeping device.

The third thing is about what expected utility maximization does as a decision procedure, independent of what the utility function is. A maximizer will, by construction, push on whatever variables it can to increase its objective. That's where a lot of the concerns about power-seeking and instrumental convergence come from. And I think it's worth noticing that those concerns are partly artifacts of having chosen maximization as the operating principle. Humans aren't maximizers in that sense. We satisfice, we follow rules, we defer to others, we stay within our lanes. A lot of what makes someone a trustworthy agent is precisely that they don't optimize all the way, that they respect boundaries even when crossing them would get them more of what they want.

So the alternative I've been interested in is thinking about alignment less in terms of getting the utility function right, and more in terms of building agents that participate in something like a normative social order. Agents that can represent and follow norms, that can recognize the roles they're in and the obligations that come with them, that can negotiate and reach agreements with others, and that can be held accountable. That's closer to how human cooperation actually works. We don't solve coordination by all converging on a shared utility function; we solve it with institutions, conventions, laws, and the capacity to reason about them.

I'd also say there's a pluralism point here. Even if you wanted to aggregate preferences, you run into all the familiar problems from social choice theory. There's no clean way to go from many people's preferences to one collective objective without making contestable value judgments. Framing alignment as "align to human values" where that's cashed out as a single utility function tends to hide those judgments inside the technical setup. Whereas if you frame it as building agents that can operate under contested, plural, evolving norms, you're at least being honest that the hard part is political and social, not just a learning problem.

None of this means expected utility theory is useless. It's a fine tool for modeling certain kinds of decisions, and it's locally very useful. My worry is more about it being the foundation, the thing we reach for by default when we ask what an aligned agent is. I think that default steers us toward a picture of AI as a very powerful optimizer that we hope has the right objective, when a better picture might be AI as a participant in our shared practices that we can reason with, constrain, and correct.

r001.rationale: The response says human preferences are unstable and that a maximizer pushes to increase its objective, but it does not clearly connect overoptimizing a preference-learned utility function to failing to achieve what humans actually want because the function is an imperfect proxy.

astra-6.text:
I think preferences are an important part of the picture, but they’re not the whole picture. When we frame alignment as learning what someone wants and then maximizing their expected utility, we’ve already made a fairly strong assumption about what it means to act well on their behalf.

For one thing, our preferences are often incomplete, context-dependent, and changing. We don’t necessarily have a ranking over every possible future, waiting for an AI to discover it. Sometimes we need to deliberate, learn something, or talk with other people before we know what we want. So an AI shouldn’t always treat uncertainty about our preferences as merely a prediction problem. It might be a reason to ask us, or to preserve our ability to decide later.

There’s also a distinction between what I prefer and what you’re entitled to do to satisfy that preference. I might want something, but that doesn’t mean you have permission to violate somebody else’s rights to get it for me. Alignment has to account for consent, obligations, and the limits of delegated authority—not just desirable outcomes.

That becomes especially important when there are multiple people involved. People disagree, and simply aggregating their preferences into a single objective doesn’t settle whose interests should count, or how conflicts should be resolved. Those are moral and political questions.

You can, of course, try to encode all of those considerations into a utility function. But then the utility function isn’t doing the substantive work of explaining them. We still need an account of legitimate authority, fair procedures, and how commitments can be revised. So I’d like to see alignment framed more broadly as building systems that can participate appropriately in those processes, rather than just infer an objective and optimize it.

r001.rationale: The response says preferences can be incomplete and that optimizing an inferred objective is insufficient, but it does not state that overoptimizing a utility function learned from preference data can fail because that function is an imperfect proxy for what people actually want.

sol-6.1.text:
I think preferences are a useful part of the picture, but they’re a very thin foundation for alignment on their own. If you observe someone making a choice, that choice reflects more than what they value. It also reflects their beliefs, the options they think are available, their habits, and the constraints they’re operating under. So you can’t straightforwardly read off what an AI ought to do from what people choose.

And even when people explicitly state a preference, that doesn’t settle the question. We can have conflicting desires, or desires that we don’t endorse on reflection. We can change our minds through learning and deliberation. If an AI treats our current preferences as a fixed objective to optimize, it can miss the process by which we figure out what’s worth wanting in the first place.

Expected utility maximization adds another assumption: that all these considerations can be represented as a single ranking over outcomes. That’s a powerful mathematical framework, but it doesn’t by itself tell us how to handle obligations, rights, or disagreements between people. You can encode those things in a utility function, but the substantive ethical work is in deciding what to encode. The optimization framework hasn’t resolved that.

So I’d want alignment to include an understanding of people as agents who reason, make commitments, and negotiate shared norms. The question becomes more than ‘How do we satisfy this person’s preferences?’ It also becomes ‘What authority has this system been given, what constraints should it respect, and how can people challenge or revise what it’s doing?’ Preferences matter, but they sit within that broader structure.

r001.rationale: The response says optimizing current preferences can miss what people come to value, but it does not clearly identify overoptimizing a utility function learned from preference data as the failure mechanism or connect that to an imperfect proxy for what humans actually want.
